danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Duellen mellem Pierre og Dolokhov blev dysset ned, og trods kejserens strenghed over for dueller på den tid slap hverken parterne eller deres sekundanter for straf. Men historien om duellen, bekræftet af Pierres brud med sin kone, var på alles læber i selskabet. Pierre, der var blevet betragtet med nedladende overbærenhed, da han var en uægte søn, og var blevet forkælet og lovprist, da han var det bedste parti i Rusland, var sunket kraftigt i selskabets anseelse efter sit ægteskab — da de gifteklare døtre og deres mødre ikke længere havde noget at håbe fra ham — især da han hverken forstod eller ønskede at søge selskabets gunst. Nu fik han alene skylden for det skete, man sagde, han var vanvittigt jaloux og havde arvet sin fars anfald af blodtørstig raseri. Og da Hélène efter Pierres afrejse vendte tilbage til Petersborg, blev hun modtaget af alle sine bekendte ikke bare hjerteligt, men endda med en anelse af ærbødighed i anledning af hendes ulykke. Når samtalen faldt på hendes mand, antog Hélène et værdigt udtryk, som hun med sin karakteristiske takt havde tilegnet sig, skønt hun ikke forstod dets betydning. Dette udtryk antydede, at hun havde besluttet at bære sine lidelser uden at klage, og at hendes mand var et kors, Gud havde lagt på hende. Fyrst Vasilij gav mere åbent udtryk for sin holdning. Han trak på skuldrene, når Pierre blev nævnt, og bemærkede med en gestus mod panden:
»Lidt berørt — det har jeg altid sagt.«

»Jeg sagde det fra begyndelsen,« erklærede Anna Pavlovna med henvisning til Pierre, »jeg sagde det dengang og før nogen anden« (hun insisterede på sin forrang) »at den tankeløse unge mand var fordærvet af vor tids fordærvede idéer. Jeg sagde det allerede dengang, da alle var henrykte over ham, da han lige var kommet hjem fra udlandet, og da han, om du husker, poserede som en slags Marat ved en af mine soiréer. Og hvad er det endt med? Jeg var imod det ægteskab allerede dengang og forudså alt, hvad der er sket.«

Anna Pavlovna fortsatte med at holde de samme slags soiréer som før på sine ledige aftener — den slags, som kun hun besad evnen til at arrangere — og hvor man fandt »fløden af det virkelig gode selskab, blomsten af Petersborgs intellektuelle essens,« som hun selv udtrykte det. Ud over dette udsøgte udvalg af selskab udmærkede Anna Pavlovnas modtagelser sig også ved, at hun altid præsenterede en ny og interessant person for gæsterne, og at ingen andre steder kunne det politiske termometer for det legitime petersborgske hofselskab aflæses så klart og tydeligt.

Hen imod slutningen af 1806, da alle de sørgelige enkeltheder om Napoleons knusning af den preussiske hær ved Jena og Auerstädt og overgivelsen af de fleste preussiske fæstninger var modtaget, da vores tropper allerede var rykket ind i Preussen, og vores anden krig mod Napoleon var begyndt, holdt Anna Pavlovna en af sine soiréer. »Fløden af det virkelig gode selskab« bestod af den fascinerende Hélène, forladt af sin mand, Mortemart, den charmerende fyrst Hippolyte (Kuragin), der netop var vendt tilbage fra Wien, to diplomater, den gamle tante, en ung mand, der i den salon blev omtalt som »en mand af stor fortjeneste«, en nyudnævnt hofdame og hendes mor samt adskillige andre mindre bemærkelsesværdige personer.

Den nyhed, Anna Pavlovna den aften havde til hensigt at servere for sine gæster, var Boris Drubetskoj, der netop var ankommet som specialkurer fra den preussiske hær og var adjutant hos en meget vigtig person.
Det politiske termometers udslag for selskabet den aften var dette:

»Hvad end de europæiske suveræner og kommandanter gør for at begunstige Bonaparte og for at volde mig og os alle vrede og krænkelse, kan vores mening om Bonaparte ikke ændres. Vi vil ikke ophøre med at give udtryk for vores oprigtige syn på sagen og kan kun sige til Preussens konge og andre: 'Desto værre for jer. Tu l'as voulu, George Dandin,' det er alt, vi har at sige om det!«

Da Boris, der skulle serveres for gæsterne, trådte ind i salonen, var næsten hele selskabet samlet, og samtalen, styret af Anna Pavlovna, drejede sig om vores diplomatiske forbindelser med Østrig og håbet om en alliance med denne magt.

Boris, der var blevet mere mandig og så frisk, rødmusset og selvsikker ud, trådte ind i salonen elegant klædt i adjutantuniform og blev behørigt ført hen for at hilse på tanten og derefter bragt tilbage til den almindelige kreds.
Anna Pavlovna rakte ham sin visnede hånd at kysse og præsenterede ham for adskillige personer, han ikke kendte, idet hun hviskende beskrev hver enkelt.

»Fyrst Hippolyte Kuragin — en charmerende ung mand; hr. Kronq — chargé d'affaires fra København — et dybt intellekt,« og ganske enkelt »hr. Sjitov — en mand af stor fortjeneste,« som det plejede at hedde om den pågældende.

Takket være Anna Mikhajlovnas (Boris' mor) anstrengelser, hans egne tilbøjeligheder og hans reserverede naturs egenart havde Boris formået under sin tjeneste at placere sig meget fordelagtigt. Han var adjutant hos en meget vigtig person, var sendt på en meget vigtig mission til Preussen og var netop vendt tilbage derfra som specialkurer. Han havde grundigt sat sig ind i den uskrevne kodeks, som han havde glædet sig over i Olmütz, og ifølge hvilken en fændrik kunne rangere usammenligneligt højere end en general, og ifølge hvilken det, der behøvedes for succes i tjenesten, ikke var flid eller arbejde, mod eller udholdenhed, men blot viden om, hvordan man kommer overens med dem, der kan tildele belønninger, og han var selv ofte forbavset over sin hurtige succes og andres manglende evne til at forstå disse ting. Som følge af denne opdagelse var hele hans levemåde, alle hans relationer til gamle venner, alle hans planer for fremtiden fuldstændig ændret. Han var ikke rig, men ville bruge sin sidste skilling for at være bedre klædt end andre og ville hellere undvære mange fornøjelser end tillade sig at blive set i en lurvet ekvipage eller vise sig på Petersborgs gader i en gammel uniform. Han blev ven med og søgte kun bekendtskab med folk, der stod over ham i rang og derfor kunne være ham til nytte. Han holdt af Petersborg og foragtede Moskva. Erindringen om familien Rostovs hus og hans barndomskærlighed til Natasja var ham ubehagelig, og han havde ikke én gang besøgt Rostoverne siden den dag, han drog af sted til hæren. At være i Anna Pavlovnas salon betragtede han som et vigtigt skridt opad i karrieren, og han forstod straks sin rolle og lod værtinden bruge den interesse, han kunne tilbyde. Han studerede selv omhyggeligt hvert ansigt, vurderede mulighederne for at knytte forbindelser med de tilstedeværende og de fordele, det kunne medføre. Han tog den plads, der var anvist ham, ved siden af den smukke Hélène og lyttede til den almindelige samtale.

»Wien anser grundlaget for den foreslåede traktat for så uopnåeligt, at end ikke de mest strålende sejre i træk ville sikre det, og man tvivler på, at vi har midlerne til at opnå dem. Det er det nøjagtige udtryk, det wienske kabinet bruger,« sagde den danske chargé d'affaires.
»Den tvivl er smigrende,« sagde »manden med det dybe intellekt« med et fint smil.
»Vi må skelne mellem det wienske kabinet og den østrigske kejser,« sagde Mortemart. »Den østrigske kejser kan aldrig have tænkt noget sådant, det er kun kabinettet, der siger det.«

»Åh, min kære vicomte,« indskød Anna Pavlovna, »L'Urope« (af en eller anden grund kaldte hun det Urope, som om det var en særlig raffineret fransk udtale, hun kunne tillade sig i samtale med en franskmand), »L'Urope ne sera jamais notre alliée sincère.«
* »Europa vil aldrig blive vores oprigtige allierede.«
Derefter førte Anna Pavlovna samtalen hen på den preussiske konges mod og fasthed for at drage Boris ind i samtalen.

Boris lyttede opmærksomt til hver af talerne, afventede sin tur, men formåede i mellemtiden gentagne gange at kaste blikke på sin sidemand, den smukke Hélène, hvis øjne flere gange mødte den flotte unge adjutants med et smil.

Anna Pavlovna spurgte ganske naturligt Boris om at fortælle dem om sin rejse til Glogau og i hvilken tilstand han fandt den preussiske hær. Boris fortalte med velovervejet tale og på rent, korrekt fransk mange interessante detaljer om hærene og hoffet, idet han omhyggeligt afholdt sig fra at udtrykke sin egen mening om de kendsgerninger, han berettede. I nogen tid fangede han den almindelige opmærksomhed, og Anna Pavlovna mærkede, at den nyhed, hun havde serveret, blev modtaget med glæde af alle hendes gæster. Den, der viste størst opmærksomhed over for Boris' beretning, var Hélène. Hun stillede ham adskillige spørgsmål om hans rejse og syntes meget interesseret i den preussiske hærs tilstand. Så snart han var færdig, vendte hun sig mod ham med sit sædvanlige smil.
»De må endelig komme og besøge mig,« sagde hun i en tone, der antydede, at det af visse grunde, han ikke kunne kende, var absolut nødvendigt.
»På tirsdag mellem otte og ni. Det vil glæde mig meget.«
Boris lovede at opfylde hendes ønske og var i færd med at indlede en samtale med hende, da Anna Pavlovna kaldte ham bort under påskud af, at hendes tante ønskede at høre ham.

»De kender jo hendes mand?« sagde Anna Pavlovna, lukkede øjnene og pegede med en bedrøvet gestus mod Hélène. »Åh, hun er en så ulykkelig og charmerende kvinde! Nævn ham ikke for hende — vær sød! Det er for smertefuldt for hende!«

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: The duel between Pierre and Dolokhov was hushed up, and despite the Emperor's strict stance on duels at that time, neither the principals nor their seconds suffered any consequences. But the story of the duel, compounded by Pierre's split with his wife, became the talk of society. Pierre — who had been treated with patronizing condescension as an illegitimate son, and then fussed over and flattered as the best match in Russia — had sunk greatly in society's estimation after his marriage, when the eligible daughters and their mothers had nothing more to hope from him — especially as he neither knew how nor wished to court public favor. Now he alone was blamed for what had happened; he was said to be insanely jealous and subject, like his father, to fits of bloodthirsty rage. And when Helene returned to Petersburg after Pierre's departure, she was received by all her acquaintances not only warmly but even with a touch of deference befitting her misfortune. When her husband came up in conversation, Helene assumed an expression of dignified composure — which, with her characteristic tact, she had cultivated despite not understanding its full significance. This expression suggested that she had resolved to bear her trials without complaint and that her husband was a cross laid upon her by God. Prince Vasili expressed his views more openly. He shrugged whenever Pierre was mentioned and, tapping his forehead, remarked:
"A bit touched — I always said so."

"I said it from the very beginning," declared Anna Pavlovna, referring to Pierre. "I said at the time, before anyone else" — she insisted on her priority — "that this reckless young man had been spoiled by the corrupt ideas of the age. I said so even when everyone was raving about him, when he had just returned from abroad and was posing as a sort of Marat at one of my soirees. And how has it ended? I was against this marriage from the start and predicted exactly what has happened."

Anna Pavlovna continued to host on her free evenings the same kind of soirees as before — the kind only she had the gift of arranging — where one could find "the cream of truly good society, the finest intellectual essence of Petersburg," as she put it. Besides this carefully curated selection, Anna Pavlovna's gatherings were also notable for the fact that she always presented some new and interesting person to the company, and that nowhere else was the political temperature of legitimate Petersburg court society so clearly and precisely registered.

Toward the end of 1806, when all the grim details had arrived of Napoleon's destruction of the Prussian army at Jena and Auerstadt and the surrender of most of the Prussian fortresses, when Russian troops had already entered Prussia and the second war with Napoleon was beginning, Anna Pavlovna held one of her soirees. The "cream of truly good society" consisted of the fascinating Helene, abandoned by her husband; Mortemart; the delightful Prince Hippolyte, just back from Vienna; two diplomats; the old aunt; a young man referred to in that drawing room as "a man of great merit"; a newly appointed maid of honor and her mother; and several other less notable guests.

The novelty Anna Pavlovna was serving up to her guests that evening was Boris Drubetskoy, who had just arrived as a special courier from the Prussian army and was aide-de-camp to a very important personage.
The temperature shown by the political thermometer that evening was as follows:

"Whatever the European sovereigns and commanders may do to appease Bonaparte, and to cause us annoyance and humiliation, our opinion of Bonaparte cannot change. We will not stop expressing our honest views on the matter, and can only say to the King of Prussia and the rest: 'So much the worse for you. Tu l'as voulu, George Dandin' — that's all we have to say about it!"

When Boris — who was to be the evening's main attraction — entered the drawing room, almost the entire company had assembled, and the conversation, guided by Anna Pavlovna, was focused on Russia's diplomatic relations with Austria and the hope of an alliance.

Boris, looking more grown-up and appearing fresh, rosy, and self-assured, entered the drawing room elegantly dressed in his aide-de-camp uniform. He was duly led over to pay his respects to the aunt and then brought back to the general circle.
Anna Pavlovna offered him her thin, shriveled hand to kiss and introduced him to several people he didn't know, giving him a whispered description of each.

"Prince Hippolyte Kuragin — charming young man. Monsieur Kronq — charge d'affaires from Copenhagen — a profound intellect." And simply: "Mr. Shitov — a man of great merit" — this of the man usually described that way.

Thanks to Anna Mikhailovna's efforts, his own instincts, and the peculiarities of his reserved temperament, Boris had managed during his military service to position himself very advantageously. He was aide-de-camp to a very important personage, had been sent on a very important mission to Prussia, and had just returned as a special courier. He had thoroughly mastered that unwritten code he had been so pleased to discover at Olmutz — the code by which an ensign could outrank a general, and success in the service depended not on effort or work, or courage or perseverance, but simply on knowing how to get along with those who dispense rewards. He was often surprised at how rapidly he advanced and at others' inability to grasp these principles. As a result, his entire manner of life, all his old friendships, all his plans for the future, had completely changed. He was not rich, but would spend his last ruble to be better dressed than others, and would sooner deny himself many pleasures than be seen in a shabby carriage or an old uniform. He cultivated friendships only with those above him in position who might be useful. He liked Petersburg and looked down on Moscow. His memories of the Rostov household and his boyhood love for Natasha were unpleasant to him, and he had not once visited the Rostovs since the day he left for the army. To be at Anna Pavlovna's drawing room he considered an important career advance, and he immediately understood his role, letting his hostess make use of whatever interest he could offer. He himself carefully assessed each face, evaluating the potential for forming connections with each person present and the advantages that might result. He took the seat indicated beside the beautiful Helene and listened to the general conversation.

"Vienna considers the terms of the proposed treaty so unattainable that not even a series of the most brilliant successes would secure them, and she doubts we have the means to achieve them. That is the exact phrase used by the Vienna cabinet," said the Danish charge d'affaires.
"The doubt is flattering," said "the man of profound intellect," with a subtle smile.
"We must distinguish between the Vienna cabinet and the Emperor of Austria," said Mortemart. "The Emperor of Austria could never have thought of such a thing; it's only the cabinet that says it."

"Ah, my dear vicomte," Anna Pavlovna chimed in, "L'Urope" — for some reason she pronounced it Urope, as if this were a specially refined French pronunciation she could permit herself when speaking with a Frenchman — "L'Urope ne sera jamais notre alliee sincere."
"Europe will never be our sincere ally."
After that, Anna Pavlovna steered the conversation to the courage and steadfastness of the King of Prussia, in order to draw Boris in.

Boris listened attentively to each speaker, waiting for his turn, but managed meanwhile to glance repeatedly at his neighbor, the beautiful Helene, whose eyes several times met the handsome young aide-de-camp's with a smile.

Speaking of Prussia's situation, Anna Pavlovna very naturally asked Boris to tell them about his trip to Glogau and the condition of the Prussian army. Boris spoke with deliberation in pure, correct French, sharing many interesting details about the armies and the court, carefully avoiding any expression of personal opinion about the facts he recounted. For some time he held everyone's attention, and Anna Pavlovna felt that the novelty she had served up was being enjoyed by all her guests. The person who paid the greatest attention to Boris's account was Helene. She asked him several questions about his travels and seemed deeply interested in the state of the Prussian army. As soon as he finished, she turned to him with her usual smile.
"You absolutely must come see me," she said in a tone implying that, for reasons he could not yet know, this was absolutely necessary.
"On Tuesday between eight and nine. It will give me great pleasure."
Boris promised to comply and was about to start a conversation with her when Anna Pavlovna called him away on the pretext that her aunt wished to hear him.

"You know her husband, of course?" said Anna Pavlovna, closing her eyes and gesturing sadly toward Helene. "Oh, she is such an unfortunate and charming woman! Don't mention him in front of her — please don't! It's too painful for her!"
